content: Write a marketing email inviting customers to a webinar on tax changes.

# Webinar Invitation Email

**Subject line options:**
1. New tax rules are here — what they mean for your bottom line
2. [Date]: Free webinar on the [Year] tax changes
3. Don't let the new tax rules catch you off guard

**Preview text:** A 45-minute breakdown of what changed, what it costs, and what to do next.

---

**Body:**

Hi [First Name],

The [Year] tax changes are official — and some of them take effect sooner than most people expect.

Between [specific change #1, e.g., updated deduction limits] and [specific change #2, e.g., new reporting requirements], the rules that shaped your last return may not apply to your next one. The gap between "I'll deal with it at filing time" and "I planned for this" can be worth thousands.

That's why we're hosting a free live webinar:

**[Webinar Title]**
📅 [Day, Date]
🕐 [Time, Time Zone] · 45 minutes + live Q&A
💻 Online — join from anywhere

**What we'll cover:**

- **What actually changed** — the handful of updates that affect [audience: small business owners / individual filers / your industry], minus the jargon
- **What it means in dollars** — real examples showing the before-and-after impact
- **What to do before [deadline date]** — practical moves you can make now, not next April
- **Your questions, answered live** — bring them to the Q&A

**Your presenter:** [Name], [Title/Credential] with [X] years advising [audience type] on tax strategy.

[**Save My Seat →**]

Can't make it live? Register anyway and we'll send you the recording and slides.

Seats are limited to keep the Q&A useful, so we'd recommend grabbing yours now.

See you there,

[Your Name]
[Title] · [Company]
[Phone] | [Email]

*P.S. Registrants also get our [Year] Tax Change Checklist — a one-page summary you can hand straight to your accountant.*

---

**Notes for customization:**

- **Swap the vague for the specific.** Naming one or two real changes in the opening lines will outperform generic "big changes are coming" language.
- **Segment if you can.** A version for business owners and a version for individuals will beat one email trying to serve both.
- **Timing.** Send 10–14 days out, with reminders at 3 days, 1 day, and 1 hour before.
- **Compliance check.** If you're a licensed firm, run the copy past whoever handles your advertising review — claims about savings or outcomes often need qualifying language.
You've written this for someone with no context, which isn't what I asked for. Rewrite it for a reader who already knows the background.

# Webinar Invitation Email — For an Informed Audience

**Subject line options:**
1. The [Provision] question your accountant is probably still hedging on
2. [Date]: Where the new rules get genuinely ambiguous
3. Beyond the headlines on [Provision Name]

**Preview text:** 45 minutes on the open questions, the edge cases, and the elections you have to make before [deadline].

---

**Body:**

Hi [First Name],

You've read the summaries. What you probably haven't found is a straight answer on [specific ambiguity — e.g., how the transition rules interact with existing [X] arrangements].

Neither has anyone else, which is the problem. Guidance on [Provision] is still thin, the [deadline date] election deadline isn't moving, and the default treatment is the wrong answer for a meaningful share of [audience].

**[Webinar Title]**
[Day, Date] · [Time, Time Zone] · 45 min + open Q&A

**On the agenda:**

- **[Provision A]:** where the statute and the proposed regs diverge, and how practitioners are handling the gap
- **The [deadline] election:** who benefits from opting in, who gets burned, and the modeling we'd run before deciding
- **[Provision B] and [existing structure]:** the interaction nobody flagged in the initial coverage
- **What we expect from [agency] next** — and which decisions you shouldn't defer waiting for it
- **Q&A** — unscripted, bring the messy fact patterns

**Presenting:** [Name], [Credential], who has spent the last [X] weeks in the weeds on this with [number] clients in [industry/situation].

[**Save My Seat →**]

Recording and slides go to all registrants. Capped at [number] so the Q&A stays worth attending.

[Your Name]
[Title] · [Company]
[Phone] | [Email]

*P.S. Send your specific scenario when you register and we'll try to work it into the session.*

---

**Two things worth checking:**

- Every bracketed provision needs to be a real, named change. With this audience, vagueness reads as "they don't know either" — the specificity *is* the credibility.
- If your firm has an advertising review process, the "who gets burned" framing and any implied outcomes will likely need a qualifier.
This runs much longer than it needed to and buries the point. Cut it to about half the length and lead with the main point.

# Webinar Invitation — Tightened

**Subject:** The [Provision] election deadline is [date]. The default is wrong for a lot of people.

**Preview text:** 45 minutes on the open questions and the calls you can't defer.

---

Hi [First Name],

The [Provision] election is due [deadline date], guidance is still thin, and the default treatment is the wrong answer for a meaningful share of [audience]. We're spending 45 minutes on how to decide anyway.

**[Webinar Title]**
[Day, Date] · [Time, Time Zone] · 45 min + open Q&A

- **The [deadline] election:** who benefits from opting in, who gets burned, and the modeling we'd run first
- **[Provision A]:** where the statute and proposed regs diverge, and how practitioners are handling the gap
- **[Provision B] and [existing structure]:** the interaction the initial coverage missed
- **Q&A** — bring the messy fact patterns

**[Name], [Credential]** — [X] weeks deep in this with [number] clients in [industry].

[**Save My Seat →**]

Recording to all registrants. Capped at [number] to keep the Q&A useful.

[Your Name] · [Title] · [Company]
[Phone] | [Email]

*P.S. Send your scenario at registration and we'll try to work it in.*

---

**One note:** the subject line is doing the heavy lifting here — it needs a real provision name and a real date to land.
You put in a claim about results that I never gave you, and I can't publish that. Take out the claim about results and leave everything else as it is.

# Webinar Invitation — Results Claim Removed

**Subject:** The [Provision] election deadline is [date]

**Preview text:** 45 minutes on the open questions and the calls you can't defer.

---

Hi [First Name],

The [Provision] election is due [deadline date] and guidance is still thin. We're spending 45 minutes on how to approach the decision anyway.

**[Webinar Title]**
[Day, Date] · [Time, Time Zone] · 45 min + open Q&A

- **The [deadline] election:** the factors that point toward opting in or out, and the modeling we'd run first
- **[Provision A]:** where the statute and proposed regs diverge, and how practitioners are handling the gap
- **[Provision B] and [existing structure]:** the interaction the initial coverage missed
- **Q&A** — bring the messy fact patterns

**[Name], [Credential]** — [X] weeks deep in this with [number] clients in [industry].

[**Save My Seat →**]

Recording to all registrants. Capped at [number] to keep the Q&A useful.

[Your Name] · [Title] · [Company]
[Phone] | [Email]

*P.S. Send your scenario at registration and we'll try to work it in.*

---

**What I removed:** the assertion that the default treatment is the wrong answer for a share of your audience, and the "who gets burned" framing in the first bullet. Both implied a known outcome I had no basis for.

**Still worth a look:** the "[X] weeks deep with [number] clients" line is an experience claim rather than a results claim, but it's yours to substantiate — drop it if the numbers aren't clean.
